title: Nudges and Their Limits

lines.text: Good afternoon. I'd like to talk about the nudge, a word that has travelled from academic journals to government departments in barely a generation, and picked up a good deal of baggage on the way.

The basic idea is simple. People don't always choose what they'd prefer if they had time to think. So, the argument goes, arrange the choices so that the sensible option is the easy one, without forbidding anything.

The classic example is the default. If employees must opt in to a pension scheme, many never get round to it. If they're enrolled automatically and must opt out, far more remain. Nobody has been compelled. The paperwork has simply been rearranged.

Studies of such schemes in several countries suggest that automatic enrolment raises participation substantially. I say 'suggest' because the size of the effect varies, and the people who stay in aren't always the people who would have chosen to.
Now, supporters call this libertarian paternalism. I confess I've never been fond of the phrase. It sounds like a political party that nobody could possibly join.
The more serious objection is about transparency. If I know that the cafeteria puts salad at eye level to improve your diet, am I being helped or handled?
Defenders reply that something has to go at eye level. There is no neutral arrangement. I find that reply clever, and I'm not entirely persuaded by it.

Because there is a difference between an arrangement that happens to favour one choice and one designed to exploit a known weakness. The first is architecture. The second is manipulation with a friendly face.

There's a further difficulty. Nudges work best on small, repeated decisions, like saving a little or taking the stairs. The large problems, such as climate or inequality, rarely yield to a clever default.
Some critics go so far as to say that nudges are a way for governments to look busy while avoiding the harder business of regulation. I think that's too cynical, but not by a wide margin.

Let me tell you what I'd actually want from a nudge. First, I'd want to be told it exists. Second, I'd want it to be easy to opt out. Third, I'd want evidence that it works for the people it's aimed at.
If those conditions are met, I see little to fear. If not, we should call it what it is, which is persuasion, and persuasion has always had its own rules.
I'm aware that this isn't a thunderous conclusion. Economists are rarely thunderous, which, as a profession, we rather like to think of as a strength.
For next week, find an example of a nudge in your own daily life, and tell me whether you think it passes my three tests.
Don't worry if you can't find one. The best nudges, by their nature, are the ones you haven't noticed.
Thank you, and do help yourselves to the salad on the way out, wherever it happens to be.

questions.explain_es: Actitud. Lo reconoce ingenioso pero no lo acepta del todo: 'I find that reply clever, and I'm not entirely persuaded by it.'

questions.explain_es: Implicatura. Más participación no equivale a elección libre: 'the people who stay in aren't always the people who would have chosen to'.

questions.explain_es: Propósito. Plantea el dilema ético: 'am I being helped or handled?'

title: The Art of Doing Very Little
focus: Restraint, understatement and humility in professional talk

lines.text: My guest today spends his days with a cotton swab and a magnifying lamp, removing, with great care, a small part of the history of art. Stefan Voss is a paintings conservator. Stefan, is it true you can spend a week on an area the size of a postage stamp?
It is, and on a bad week, two. People expect a conservator to work like a restorer in a film, sweeping in with a brush and a flourish. Mostly we sit still and think.
What are you thinking about?
Mostly, what not to do. The first rule is that anything we add must be reversible. If a better method is invented in fifty years, our successors shouldn't have to undo our enthusiasm.
That seems very modest for a profession dealing with masterpieces.

It's less modesty than realism. Every generation of restorers has been certain that it was improving things, and many of them did damage in the process. I try to remember that I'm part of a long line of confident people.
Can you give an example of that damage?

Over-cleaning is the classic. A painting develops a yellowed varnish over the years, and it's tempting to take it all off to reveal the bright colours. But sometimes the artist painted in the expectation of a layer of varnish, and strip it and you've changed the picture.
So how do you know when to stop?
You don't, quite. You make a judgement, you document it, and you leave the painting in a state somebody can revisit. I'd say about half of my skill is knowing how little to do.
There's a famous debate about whether a restored painting should look new or look old.
There is, and I think both camps are slightly missing the point. The aim isn't to make a painting look young. It's to let you see what the artist intended without lying about its age.
What happens when the damage is severe, when part of a painting has simply gone?

We fill the loss, but in a way that's discernible from close up. From a metre away it reads as continuous; from nearer, you can see where I've been. That's my signature, if you like, in invisible ink.
A signature nobody is supposed to read.
Exactly. The ideal conservator is a ghost with excellent handwriting.
Is there ever a painting you'd rather not have touched?

Once or twice. A small portrait I was asked to clean turned out to be far more fragile than the records suggested. I spent a month deciding whether to proceed, and in the end I did very little. The owner was disappointed. I thought it was the right decision.
Stefan Voss, thank you.
Thank you. Do keep your distance from the paintings when you visit; I'd like to keep my job.

questions.q: What is Stefan's attitude to earlier generations of restorers?
options: Contempt for their lack of training
Humble awareness that confidence has caused harm
Pride in belonging to an infallible tradition
Anxiety that no one will trust his own work
questions.explain_es: Actitud. Reconoce con humildad errores pasados: 'many of them did damage in the process. I try to remember that I'm part of a long line of confident people.'

questions.q: What does he imply by saying that half of his skill is 'knowing how little to do'?
options: He often leaves jobs unfinished

Most paintings need very little work
questions.explain_es: Implicatura. La contención es parte central del oficio: 'about half of my skill is knowing how little to do'.

questions.q: Stefan says that the fill-in work can be seen when viewers stand close.
questions.explain_es: Detalle. Dice: 'in a way that's discernible from close up'.

questions.q: Why does he describe the yellowed varnish?
options: To illustrate how over-cleaning can alter a picture
To prove that varnish never yellows
To explain how cotton swabs are made
To recommend removing varnish from every painting
questions.explain_es: Propósito. Ejemplifica el riesgo de limpiar en exceso: 'strip it and you've changed the picture'.

questions.q: What does the image 'a ghost with excellent handwriting' convey?
options: A fear of haunted galleries

Skilled work that is meant to go unnoticed
questions.explain_es: Ironía. Es una imagen humorística del conservador: hábil pero invisible, como la 'invisible ink' de su firma.

questions.explain_es: Detalle. Dice: 'in the end I did very little'.

dictation: Mostly we sit still and think.

title: Concrete Feelings

lines.text: Welcome to Built Environment. Tonight, a style that people either love or want demolished: brutalism. Marcus Bell is an architect who has restored several brutalist buildings; Yuki Tanaka is a critic who, I gather, has not enjoyed all of them. Yuki, why is brutalist architecture so divisive?

Because it's honest to a fault. The name, by the way, comes from the French for raw concrete, beton brut, not from any wish to be brutal. The buildings show how they're made. Some people find that refreshing. Others feel they're being shouted at.
I'd say they're being addressed plainly, which in a world of glass and cladding feels almost rude.
Rude is the word. There's something quite defiant about a building that makes no effort to charm you.
And yet many of them were built with generous intentions. Housing, universities, libraries. The idealism is easy to miss behind the weathered grey.
I wouldn't deny the intentions. I'd question the results. A good many estates promised community and delivered corridors where nobody knew their neighbour.
That's partly because the maintenance money ran out. Concrete isn't the problem. A building that is never cleaned, never repaired and never loved will look grim, whatever it's made of.
A convenient defence, if I may say so. You can excuse any design by blaming the budget.
I'd put it differently. You can condemn any design by blaming the materials.
Marcus, you've worked on restoring these buildings. What do you find?
Often, to my surprise, that people who live in them are fond of them. They talk about the light, the thickness of the walls, the way a corridor can feel like a street.
Residents, I'd note, are a self-selecting group. Those who hate it have often moved.
Quite possibly. Though I'd gently suggest that the critics are also self-selecting.
Yuki, will you concede anything?

I'll concede that demolishing a building should be the last resort rather than the first. A structure that has taken enormous energy to make carries that energy with it. It's no small thing to throw away.
Now that, if I may say so, is an argument I'd have expected from me.
I thought I'd confuse you.
On which note of mutual surprise, we'll take a short break.

questions.q: What is Yuki's attitude to Marcus's defence that blame lies with the budget?
options: Hostile: she feels he has insulted her
Enthusiastic: she agrees fully with his reasoning
Sceptical: she suspects it excuses any design
Indifferent: budgets do not interest her
questions.explain_es: Actitud. Lo ve como una excusa cómoda: 'A convenient defence, if I may say so. You can excuse any design by blaming the budget.'

questions.q: What does Marcus imply by saying that 'the critics are also self-selecting'?
options: Residents' opinions are worthless
Critics have never lived in such buildings

Self-selection only affects residents
questions.explain_es: Implicatura. Devuelve el argumento: si los residentes están sesgados, los críticos también lo están.

questions.q: Marcus says that residents of brutalist buildings often like the light inside.
questions.explain_es: Detalle. Dice: 'They talk about the light, the thickness of the walls'.

questions.q: Why does Yuki mention where the name 'brutalism' comes from?
options: To show that she is fluent in French
To correct a misunderstanding about the name
To argue that raw concrete is unsafe
To claim the label began as an insult
questions.explain_es: Propósito. Corrige la idea de que el estilo busca ser brutal: 'not from any wish to be brutal'.

questions.q: What is the tone of Yuki's last remark, 'I thought I'd confuse you'?
options: Apologetic about changing her view
Solemn, ending the debate
Playful, enjoying having surprised him
Angry that he interrupted her
questions.explain_es: Ironía. Bromea sobre haber sorprendido a Marcus con un argumento que él habría defendido.

questions.explain_es: Detalle. Dice: 'demolishing a building should be the last resort rather than the first'.

dictation: A building that is never cleaned, never repaired and never loved will look grim, whatever it's made of.

title: In Praise of the Complaint Letter

lines.text: Good evening. I'd like to say a few words in praise of the complaint letter, an art form now sadly in decline, like the telegram and the dignified sulk.
Anyone can complain. Shouting at a call centre is a form of complaining, in the same sense that a toddler throwing a spoon is a form of cuisine. The letter requires craft.
Rule one is to begin with praise. I always open by saying that I have been a loyal customer for many years, which has the double merit of being slightly true and entirely beside the point.

Rule two is to be specific. 'The service was poor' will be filed under 'noted'. But 'on the fourth of March, a man named Kevin told me my parcel was in the building, in a tone suggesting it had moved in permanently' will be read aloud in the office.
Rule three is the most delicate: never be rude. Rudeness is a gift to the recipient. It allows them to feel wronged, and, in practice, to ignore you.
Instead, use the terrible weapon of politeness. 'I was somewhat surprised' is far more alarming than 'I was furious', and 'I'm sure this is an oversight' has ended careers.

I'm told some companies employ a department of replies, staffed by gentle people trained to say 'We are sorry you feel this way'. You will have noticed the genius of the phrase. It apologises for your feelings and for nothing else.
Rule four is to know what you want. A complaint without a request is merely a diary entry.

The resolution, when it comes, is usually a voucher. I have received vouchers for hotels I'd never visit, restaurants I've never heard of and, on one memorable occasion, a discount on a mattress I'd specifically complained about.
I'm not suggesting that this is a victory. I'm suggesting it's an education.
Because here is the thing. Beneath the comedy, a good complaint is an act of faith. You write because you believe that somewhere a person might read it, and be moved to improve things.
It is a ridiculous belief, and the world runs on it. If nobody ever complained, nobody would ever have the chance to be corrected.

There was a bus company once, near my home, whose timetable was a work of fiction. I wrote to them eleven times, politely. In the end they changed the timetable. I like to think it was my doing, though it may have been the new manager.
Even so, I'm fond of the idea that it was me. Every small bureaucracy needs a dedicated, courteous irritant, and I am proud to serve.
So let me leave you with a challenge. The next time something goes wrong, don't shout, don't post an angry review, and don't sigh into your tea. Write a letter.
And if it fails, you have lost nothing but a stamp, and gained a story. Thank you for listening, and I do hope you'll all write to tell me what you thought.

options: Bitter disappointment at its failure
Strict disapproval of unhappy customers
Weary indifference to company replies
Fond respect, expressed with humour
questions.explain_es: Actitud. La defiende con cariño y humor: 'a few words in praise of the complaint letter' y 'The letter requires craft'.

options: The reply is too short to be polite

questions.explain_es: Implicatura. La fórmula no asume responsabilidad: 'It apologises for your feelings and for nothing else.'

questions.explain_es: Detalle. Dice: 'I was somewhat surprised' is far more alarming than 'I was furious'.

options: To suggest that she never complains again

questions.explain_es: Propósito. Ilustra una compensación absurda: 'a discount on a mattress I'd specifically complained about'.

title: What Do We Not Hear?

lines.text: Good morning. Please indulge me for thirty seconds. Close your eyes and listen to this room. I'll wait. What did you hear that you hadn't noticed when you walked in?
Most of you, I suspect, heard the ventilation, perhaps a distant door, perhaps your own breathing. None of it was new. It was simply unattended.
That, in a sentence, is the problem of noise. It isn't only a matter of loudness. It's a matter of what we've learned to filter out, and at what price.
Take your commute. Sirens, engines, the wheeze of a bus door, and, I'd guess, a good deal of music piped into your ears to drown it all out.

In the nineteen seventies, researchers in Canada began recording the sounds of cities as carefully as naturalists catalogue birds. They argued that a place has a sound identity, just as it has a skyline, and that we neglect it at our peril.

The public-health case is better established. Research over many years has associated chronic exposure to loud environmental noise, such as road and air traffic, with sleep disturbance and a higher risk of heart disease. I say 'associated' because proving cause is hard, but the pattern is consistent.
There is also the less measurable matter of mood. People living on noisy streets report more irritability and less sense of control. It's the sense of control that interests me.

Because a sound you choose and a sound imposed on you can be identical in volume and utterly different in effect. A teenager's music at a concert is a pleasure. The same music through a wall at midnight is a grievance.
This is why measuring noise in decibels alone is a blunt instrument. A fountain and a pneumatic drill might register similarly. Nobody would confuse the experience.
So what might a better approach look like? Some cities have begun to treat quiet as a public resource, mapping areas of relative calm and protecting them, much as one would a park.

Others are experimenting with the opposite: adding sounds. Water features, birdsong played through speakers, even rustling leaves. I confess I find the last of these faintly ridiculous, and I'm not sure why I find it more ridiculous than a lawn that is mown for the look of it.

I'd offer a note of caution about the technological fix. If we simply mask unpleasant sound with pleasant sound, we may feel better without addressing the cause. A pleasant noise is not a cure for a road.
What I'm really arguing for is attention. Not silence, which is rare, expensive and slightly eerie, but a habit of noticing what we hear and asking who chose it.
For your assignment, take a fifteen-minute walk without headphones and write down every sound. You'll be surprised by how much is there, and by how little you've been hearing.
I'd also invite you to notice what you can't hear. The quiet corners of a city are often where the interesting people are hiding.
Thank you. I hope you'll all spend the rest of the day listening a little more suspiciously.

options: Anger at wasted public money
Mild amusement mixed with self-doubt

questions.explain_es: Actitud. Le parece algo ridículo pero duda de su propia reacción: 'I find the last of these faintly ridiculous, and I'm not sure why'.

questions.q: What does she imply by saying that 'a pleasant noise is not a cure for a road'?

questions.explain_es: Implicatura. Tapar el ruido no elimina su causa: 'we may feel better without addressing the cause'.

questions.q: She says that a chosen sound and an imposed sound can differ greatly in effect even at the same volume.
questions.explain_es: Detalle. Dice: 'can be identical in volume and utterly different in effect'.

questions.q: Why does she begin by asking the audience to close their eyes and listen?
options: To introduce the exam format
To demonstrate how much we habitually ignore
To calm an anxious audience
To test the students' hearing
questions.explain_es: Propósito. Demuestra que hay sonidos que no atendemos: 'None of it was new. It was simply unattended.'

questions.q: How should her closing wish about listening 'more suspiciously' be understood?
options: As a serious accusation against students
As a warning that the city is dangerous
As a complaint about the noise in the room
As a light remark urging closer attention
questions.explain_es: Ironía. Es una broma ligera con un fin serio: pedir más atención al entorno sonoro.

questions.q: She says that research has proved that traffic noise directly causes heart disease.
questions.explain_es: Detalle. Dice 'associated' y añade: 'proving cause is hard'.

dictation: A pleasant noise is not a cure for a road.

title: Should Machine-Written Text Carry a Label?

lines.text: Welcome. Tonight's motion: any text substantially written by a machine should carry a visible label. Omar Haddad, an editor, supports it. Fiona Walsh, who studies media law, opposes. Omar, begin.

Thank you. My case is simple: readers have a right to know who, or what, is speaking to them. We label food, we label advertising, and we expect a byline on a newspaper article. I fail to see why this should be the exception.

That's a tidy analogy, but food labels describe ingredients with legal definitions. 'Substantially written by a machine' has none. Is a spell-checked paragraph labelled? A translated one? A paragraph that a person wrote and a machine tidied?
A fair challenge. I'd say the line is drawn wherever a reasonable reader would feel misled. That's how fraud law works, after all.
Which concedes my point, because 'a reasonable reader' is exactly the kind of judgement that courts argue about for years.
I'd rather they argued than that readers were left wholly in the dark.
Fiona, you've said the label would be unworkable. Is that your main objection?

My main objection is that it would be both unenforceable and misleading. The honest will label, the dishonest won't, and the public will come to trust unlabelled text as human. That's worse than the present confusion.
I notice you've framed the entire argument as a defence of the dishonest.
On the contrary, I'm defending the reader against false reassurance. A label that only the well-behaved bother to apply protects nobody.
Rather like a seatbelt that only the careful wear.
Seatbelts are mandatory, Omar, and the comparison has just done my work for me. If you want enforcement, say so plainly, and tell us who will do the policing.
I will. A regulator, with proportionate fines, and with powers to inspect. I accept it isn't glamorous.
Fiona, would any version of labelling be acceptable to you?
A narrow one. Labels for specific high-risk settings, such as medical advice or political advertising, where a mistake could really hurt people. That I could support.
Then we're closer than the motion suggests. I'd accept a narrower rule as a start, provided it isn't also the end.
Provided it isn't also the end. I'll note that for my next speech, which I suspect will be longer.
I'm sure it will. We'll now open the floor.

options: He blames his opponent's lack of preparation
He concedes the difficulty yet keeps his position
He dismisses the difficulty as imaginary
He abandons the motion entirely
questions.explain_es: Actitud. Admite el reto pero mantiene su postura: 'A fair challenge. I'd say the line is drawn wherever a reasonable reader would feel misled.'

He thinks she is personally dishonest
questions.explain_es: Implicatura. Insinúa que su postura beneficia a quienes engañan, aunque no lo diga abiertamente.

questions.q: Fiona would accept labels in some high-risk settings.
questions.explain_es: Detalle. Dice: 'Labels for specific high-risk settings, such as medical advice or political advertising ... That I could support.'

questions.q: Why does Fiona say that the seatbelt comparison 'has just done my work for me'?
options: To agree that voluntary labels would work
To end the debate in her favour
To argue that seatbelts are unnecessary
To push him to say who would enforce the rule
questions.explain_es: Propósito. Un cinturón obligatorio implica control; le exige concretar quién vigilará: 'tell us who will do the policing'.

options: Humble, admitting she lacks arguments

title: The Voice Nobody Notices

lines.text: Most of us only notice an interpreter when something goes wrong, which is a curious fate for a profession whose whole purpose is to be understood. Hana Lindgren interprets at international conferences. Hana, what does a good day look like?
A good day is one where nobody thanks me. If the delegates leave remembering what the minister said and not who translated it, I've done my job.
That seems a thankless ambition.
It's a thankless profession, in the nicest sense. We choose it knowing the best compliment is silence.
How do you do it? You listen and speak at once.

With difficulty, and with a partner. In simultaneous work we take turns, usually every twenty to thirty minutes, because the concentration is so intense that accuracy falls away after that. The colleague who's resting still follows along and passes notes, mostly numbers and names.
Why numbers?
Because they're the one thing you can't paraphrase. If a speaker says forty-seven million and I say forty-seven thousand, nobody's going to forgive me by pointing at the general sense.
And humour? Jokes must be a nightmare.

They're the nightmare. A joke is built on a particular word or a shared reference, and it rarely survives the journey. The usual solution is to say, 'The speaker has made a joke; please laugh.' It never works, and everyone laughs out of politeness.
Which, I suppose, is itself a joke.
A gentle one. I don't take credit.
What happens when a speaker says something offensive or untrue? Do you soften it?
No. That's a fundamental rule. I'm not there to improve anyone. If a speaker is rude, I'm rude in the other language. It can be uncomfortable, and occasionally the delegates give me an accusing look.
As though you'd said it yourself.
Precisely. I've learned to keep a neutral face and a clear conscience.
Do you think machines will take over?

For routine material, they're already surprisingly capable. For a tense negotiation, where one hesitation or one word choice can shift a meeting, I'd be uneasy handing over responsibility. At least for the foreseeable future.
And do you ever dream in two languages?
Constantly, and usually the wrong one at the wrong moment. Last month I answered the waiter in the language I'd interpreted all day. He was very patient.
Hana Lindgren, thank you, and I'm told that was entirely your own words.
Every one of them. Or so I'd like to think.

questions.q: What is Hana's attitude to going unnoticed in her work?
options: She treats being unnoticed as a sign of success
She resents the lack of public thanks
She blames delegates for ignoring her
She hopes to become well known
questions.explain_es: Actitud. Lo ve como señal de éxito: 'A good day is one where nobody thanks me.'

questions.q: What does Hana imply by saying that nobody would forgive an error with numbers 'by pointing at the general sense'?
options: She often invents numbers when unsure

questions.explain_es: Implicatura. Las cifras no admiten aproximación: 'they're the one thing you can't paraphrase'.

questions.q: Hana says that machines are already quite capable with routine material.
questions.explain_es: Detalle. Dice: 'For routine material, they're already surprisingly capable.'

questions.q: Why does Hana say that she renders rudeness faithfully?
options: To show how rarely speakers are rude
To confess that she enjoys being rude
To warn speakers about insulting delegates
To stress that her role is to convey, not to edit
questions.explain_es: Propósito. Subraya su papel de transmisora fiel: 'I'm not there to improve anyone.'

questions.q: What does Hana imply about the 'please laugh' technique for jokes?
options: It conveys the joke fully

questions.explain_es: Ironía. Resulta cómico porque nadie se ríe de verdad: 'everyone laughs out of politeness'.

dictation: A good day is one where nobody thanks me.

title: Fast News, Slow News
focus: Concession, gentle irony and balanced argument

lines.text: Welcome to The Media Hour. Tonight, the question of speed. Ravi Menon edits a quarterly magazine that publishes four long investigations a year. Anneke de Vries reports for a rolling news channel and has, by her own estimate, filed about nine stories before lunch. Ravi, why slow?

Because some stories can't be told quickly without being told wrongly. A scandal in a council contract takes months to establish. The first account is nearly always partial, and the corrections never travel as far as the original.
I agree with half of that. The first account is partial, and it should say so. But there's a public interest in knowing something is happening now, not in a quarter's time.
Is there? If you tell me a fire is spreading, I'm grateful. If you tell me, forty minutes in, why it started, I'd rather you waited.

That's a distinction I'd happily accept. The trouble is that the pressure to speculate comes from the audience as much as from editors. People refresh a page every minute and are cross when nothing's changed.
So who's to blame, the public or the press?
A bit of both. Which is the tidy answer you'd expect from someone paid to be balanced.
I resent that, mildly.
I'd say the economics matter most. Speed is cheap and slowness is expensive. A reporter who spends three months on a story has not written anything else, and someone has to pay for that.
And the ones who pay are readers, who in my experience are keener on the idea of slow journalism than on the subscription.
A shrewd observation, and a painful one.
Anneke, can speed ever be a virtue?

When people are in danger, certainly. During a flood, information is a kind of rescue. I've seen a clear warning, sent at the right moment, get a whole valley moving to higher ground. I wouldn't trade that for any number of beautiful long reads.
Nor would I, and I'd be a fraud if I claimed otherwise. My objection is to the idea that every story is a flood.
Rather well put. And rather annoying, because I'd been planning to say it.
Does either of you read the other's work?
Every day, and with a mixture of admiration and professional envy. She finishes before I've started.
And his stories make mine look like the first draft of a sketch. I'm not sure whether that's a compliment to him or a confession from me.
Probably both. Thank you, both. That's all we have time for.

questions.q: What is Ravi's attitude to the first account of a breaking story?
options: He believes corrections spread widely
He values it above later reports
He ignores it as irrelevant
He distrusts it as incomplete
questions.explain_es: Actitud. Desconfía de los primeros relatos: 'The first account is nearly always partial, and the corrections never travel as far as the original.'

questions.q: What does Anneke imply by calling 'A bit of both' the 'tidy answer you'd expect from someone paid to be balanced'?
options: She refuses to answer the question
She jokes that her answer is predictably diplomatic
She places all blame on the audience
She accuses the chair of bias
questions.explain_es: Implicatura. Se ríe de su propia respuesta, diplomática por oficio: 'a tidy answer ... from someone paid to be balanced'.

questions.q: Ravi accepts that speed matters when a flood threatens.
questions.explain_es: Detalle. Responde a Anneke: 'Nor would I, and I'd be a fraud if I claimed otherwise.'

questions.q: Why does Anneke describe the flood warning?
options: To prove that readers prefer short stories
To show that speed can save lives
To criticise the quality of rolling news
To complain about her own workload
questions.explain_es: Propósito. Defiende el valor de la rapidez: 'During a flood, information is a kind of rescue.'

questions.q: What does Anneke imply when she says readers are 'keener on the idea of slow journalism than on the subscription'?
options: Subscriptions are too cheap to matter
Slow journalism has too few readers to need money
Readers prefer to subscribe to news channels
Readers admire slow journalism without paying for it
questions.explain_es: Ironía. Los lectores elogian el periodismo lento pero no lo pagan; Ravi lo llama 'A shrewd observation, and a painful one'.

questions.q: Anneke says her channel files only a few stories each day.
questions.explain_es: Detalle. Ha archivado 'about nine stories before lunch'.

dictation: Speed is cheap and slowness is expensive.
My objection is to the idea that every story is a flood.
